Maintainer block (L92-109) carries dated Quality/Source-verification stamps and forward-looking fallback clauses ('drop the single attribution', 'reframe as unattributed'), no journey verbs (settled/retired/restored/renamed/was changed to) describing a completed transition -- stays inside the dated-provenance carve-out. rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Machine-cadence fat — the shape of good prose without the content.
rules_evaluated.evidence: (a) Empty negation: closest is L46 'if two sessions open the same working directory (not two worktrees, the same folder)' -- negates a real, plausible misreading (that the trap is about separate worktree folders), a needed disambiguation. The rewritten L11 ('Nothing committed is silently overwritten') is a positive scoped claim, not an 'X, not Y' shape, so it doesn't trip this sub-rule. (b) Deictic drumroll: L29 'That creates a sibling directory...' and L74 'This is the one place the human stays in the driver seat' both resolve a real antecedent (legitimate per the rule's own test). (c) Bold-label echo: L19/21/23 '**Branches** are cheap.'/'**Clones** are heavy.'/'**Worktrees** are the middle path.' -- the bold word is the sentence's own subject, not a restated label followed by a new sentence repeating the noun; not an echo. rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Don't state a count the adjacent list already holds.
rules_evaluated.evidence: L17: 'Three ways to have "another copy of this code to work on." They behave differently.' sits directly above the three bold-lead paragraphs that follow (L19 Branches / L21 Clones / L23 Worktrees) -- the exact banned shape, and this file's own sibling instance of the same pattern (formerly at L80, 'Three situations where one session beats three') has already been fixed elsewhere in this file's history to 'Situations where one session beats three' (current L78), confirming the pattern is recognized and fixable without loss. This L17 instance was left unfixed across the pinned diff -- `git diff 0cea7581..HEAD` touched L11, L54, and the Quality line only, not L17. The numeral is never reused as a memory handle elsewhere in the file, so the across-distance carve-out doesn't rescue it -- the items are visible in the very next lines. Harm: a fourth means of duplicating a repo added later (e.g. sparse-checkout) silently falsifies 'Three', invisible to an editor working on the list, not the sentence above it. Non-blocking per the rule's own default (this is style guidance, not a hard-grep item).
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: Drop the numeral: 'Ways to have "another copy of this code to work on." They behave differently.'

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: A slogan that is false as stated is not punchy framing — run the truth test before reaching for §12.
rules_evaluated.evidence: The pinned diff (`git diff 0cea7581..HEAD`) rewrote L11 from 'Nothing silently overwrites.' to 'Nothing committed is silently overwritten.' This resolves the prior finding against this file: the old unscoped absolute contradicted L46's 'the agent-level trap' (two sessions in the same working directory, 'the later write wins... the earlier session's in-progress edit gets clobbered on disk'). That trap is about UNCOMMITTED, same-folder filesystem writes -- a raw clobber Git never sees -- not about committed/merge-tracked work. The new wording scopes the absolute to 'committed' work specifically, and committed Git objects genuinely are never silently overwritten (force-push/reset requires a deliberate act, and Git itself always surfaces a merge collision, per L11's preceding sentence). Read against L46 with the new scoping, there is no remaining counterexample in this file.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Say it once, at its most concrete, then at most one sentence that generalises it. Style, not a gate.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Closest candidate for shape (d), the second announcement: L11 'If two sessions collide, Git tells you at merge time' and L73 'Git tells you. Both sessions will stop and show you the conflict markers.' restate the same underlying fact (Git surfaces conflicts) in two different sections. But this is the rule's own named exception -- 'a deliberate second pass at a genuinely hard idea is legitimate' -- not a flaw: L11 sits in the 'Why multi-session, why Git' overview making a one-clause promise, and L70-76 is the dedicated 'Conflict recovery' section cashing that promise with the actual mechanism (conflict markers, don't auto-resolve, read the diff). Checked the other three shapes: (a) no abstract-twin pair found -- L13's three sentences (claim, mechanism, concrete outcome) each add new information rather than restating one idea at two altitudes; (b) no prose restates an adjacent fence's own content (the fence blocks at L25-27/50-52/60-64 are followed only by explanation the command syntax doesn't itself state); (c) no widening qualifier ('or rule', 'or context-dependent') found anywhere in body.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Aspirational destination, never corrective gap.
rules_evaluated.evidence: No corrective-gap framing ('you're missing Y') anywhere. Closest tier-adjacent line: L84-86 item 3, '**New to the loop.** If you are still learning what "good" looks like in one session, adding a second session adds variables, not learning.' -- conditional ('if'), non-pejorative, one of three parallel situational reasons to prefer one session, not a fixed tier assigned to the reader. No 'at your scale'/'for a beginner'/'a senior would already know' phrasing. Pre-prompt-check sub-rule N/A: this reference file has no pre-flight/readiness gate.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Earn every technical term on first use.
rules_evaluated.evidence: worktree earned L13 ('Worktrees are the Git feature that makes multi-session fast... one per branch, each in its own folder'); clone earned L21; stash earned L58 ('git stash is how work moves between sessions'); branch earned L19. rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Golden path only in body — THIS RULE HAS AN EXCEPTION; read to the boundary before cutting anything.
rules_evaluated.evidence: The file's entire back half is recovery content by design ('Conflict recovery when two sessions edited the same file', 'When NOT to run multi-session'), plus the renamed L54 section explicitly naming 'small recoveries' -- squarely inside the rule's own boundary: a plausible failure (merge collisions, wrong-branch commits, and mis-scoped parallelism are the expected failure modes of the exact workflow being taught) with a non-obvious rescue (don't let the agent auto-resolve; read the diff yourself; `git reset --soft HEAD~1`), stated next to the risk, not routed to a maintainer-only surface a student in delivery never reaches. The title frames the whole file as a 'survival guide' -- recovery is the golden path here.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Don't ask student to manually diff or spot-check Claude's output as error-catching.
rules_evaluated.evidence: L74-76's 'Read the diff. Pick which line wins, or write the line that reconciles both.' names both object (the diff -- exempt per the rule's own example, 'the diff is the artifact') and tell (pick or write the reconciling line), and states the reason it can't be delegated ('agents are confident and do not always read carefully enough at a merge boundary'). This is a two-sided git conflict where both changes may be legitimate and only the human knows intent, not error-catching on the agent's output. No un-addressed speech verb, no unknowable criterion, no fictional gate anywhere in body.
